subject: The measured gains, correctness risks and costs of reducing repeated TD text drawing and hidden output callbacks.
reader: Parker owns and uses Terminal Delight with many coding agents. He authorized fixes and wants measured gains, tradeoffs and uncertainties in plain English, without reading Rust.

sections.heading: Less work between changes
sections.text:
TD now reuses quiet panes’ text drawing and skips screen-update messages from hidden panes. In the mixed-pane test, window CPU fell 29% . The main cost is retained memory; the main uncertainty is how much your changing mix of agents benefits. 

 Measured on this machine Verified release · paired measurements and native checks complete About six minutes · details unfold below

sections.heading: 01 The gain
sections.text:
You asked for the remaining savings in drawing and busy hidden panes. Both had avoidable work. These measurements compare the new changes with the already-optimized build, so earlier savings are not counted again.

 Retaining quiet text saves CPU when another pane changes. Dots show every paired observation; bars show medians. Four panes shared each test window. The hidden test used thirty synthetic agent panes behind one quiet tab. These are TD window measurements; agent computation and the rest of the desktop are outside these bars. Plain hidden programs saved 1.4 points at the median. Synthetic agents improved in 6 of 10 pairs; that noisier result does not establish a dependable agent-workload gain. 

The benefit needs an explanation beyond a lower number. A profile of the old drawing path showed where to look.

sections.heading: 02 Repeated layout
sections.text:
02 One changing pane made quiet text expensive Measured 

At least 51% laying out elements 
49% other sampled work 

 Changing at 20 Hz working 00000416▌ 
 Quiet unchanged text 
 Quiet unchanged text 
 Quiet unchanged text 

 The window kept laying out rows that had not changed. In a separate 20-second profile, 406 samples from the main drawing thread included at least 50.99% in layout functions. This is a share of sampled thread work, not a prediction of total CPU savings. The live-session profile had only nineteen samples and was too sparse to rank causes. 

Keeping a whole pane’s drawing would skip important work: its position must be registered each frame for TD’s distortion effects. The fix therefore retains only the text grid. 

 03 The reuse boundary Code and tests 

Pane header, input handling and geometry run each frame 

 Terminal text 
 Same painted rows
and geometry → Reuse layout
and drawing 
 Text, cursor, selection,
colour or size changes → Draw fresh
in this frame 

Pictures, documents, overlays and effects keep their own paths 

 Unchanged text is reused while the pane stays interactive. The comparison uses the final rows people see, including the cursor, selection and colours. Geometry and inherited text style also participate in the drawing library’s checks. This is checked by render and invalidation tests. Whole-pane reuse was rejected because it could skip per-frame effect registration.

sections.heading: 03 Hidden output
sections.text:
Text reuse helps visible panes. A hidden pane has another cost: each chunk of output used to send the interface a message even though there was nothing to show. 

 04 Output keeps arriving; needless screen messages stop Code and tests 

Agent writes output ↓ 
Terminal parses it
 latest text and scrollback stay current ↓ 

 Screen changed 
Hidden: record the change.
Use the existing clock.
Shown: draw current text. 
 Protocol or state event 
Colour request, title, bell, exit:
continue through immediately. 

 1 second hidden housekeeping, unchanged 5 seconds background refresh, unchanged On activation read the latest grid 

 This removes interface wakeups without slowing the terminal parser. The test sends forty writes separately, confirms each reached the grid, and observes zero screen callbacks while hidden. A title still arrives before the test clock advances. Existing protocol, prompt, completion and resize tests remain in place. No new sleeping interval was introduced. 

Both changes depend on recognizing when reuse is unsafe. That is where the tests had to challenge the implementation.

sections.heading: 04 What failed
sections.text:
05 The tests rejected stale drawing and missing savings Observed failures 

 First cache design 
Update the retained view during its parent’s draw. New text and cursor tests failed. The drawing library had already collected that frame’s invalidations. → 
 Corrected design 
Replace the retained view when the final painted content changes. Fresh drawing in the same frame. Identical content keeps the previous view. 

 Disable text reuse Quiet-grid test fails 
 Restore hidden wakeups Hidden-output test fails 

 Passing tests alone were insufficient. Deliberately removing both optimizations caused the two intended failures; 246 other pane tests still passed. The source was then restored and checked. Native testing also exercised real tab activation, documents and a window restart against the old terminal host, preserving both shell identities. The integrated release suites passed 2,465 default-core tests and 2,418 alternate-core tests, with nine ignored in each. 

Correctness tests explain why the changes are safe enough to ship. The unfavorable workloads and memory measurements decide whether they are worth keeping.

sections.heading: 05 Cost and uncertainty
sections.text:
06 What we pay for the reduction 
 | 
 | Tradeoff | What the evidence says 

 | Memory | One mixed run showed +12.5 MiB for the new window; reversing launch order showed −1.2 MiB. Two identical old builds differed by +47.4 MiB. The added storage is one retained text viewport per rendered pane; its resident-memory cost remains unresolved. The measurement includes allocator and renderer state, so it cannot isolate the text cache’s exact size. 

 | Busy panes | At 100 updates per second in each of four panes, window CPU went from 20.7% to 16.4% of one core, with improvement in all five pairs. Comparing rows and making a new view still cost work when text changes. The stress test checks that cost under continuous output. 

 | Timing bias | Two identical old builds differed by -0.12 to +0.25 CPU points across five pairs. Reversing launch order gave a 29.1% median paired reduction. Both binaries used equal window sizes on the same isolated display. 

 | User experience | Fresh output, selection, cursor, scrolling, palette changes and resizing pass the tests. Typing latency and frame-time tails were not measured; unchanged scheduling alone does not prove they are identical. 

 | Unknown | Whole-machine CPU reduction, battery life and the benefit during your actual day remain unmeasured. CRT effects were off in the controlled tests. 

 The gain is specific to these workloads. Tests ran on a temporary headless output while the physical displays stayed asleep and the desktop remained locked. Windows rendered there, and a native capture verified fresh text. This controls the comparison; it does not reproduce every compositor, animation or agent workload you use. 

The least certain engineering choice was replacing the cached view on every content change. It guarantees fresh drawing, but costs allocation. The busy-pane measurements above are the direct check on that tradeoff. 

 07 An earlier fix still awaits a new terminal host CPU attribution 

 TD window 
Drawing and interface updates.
Can be replaced while shells keep running. 
 Process keeping terminals alive 
The live host still runs older code.
Its conversation lookup can read whole files. 

 Old lookup reads the whole candidate file New lookup reads its first 4 KiB Current sessions kept alive 

 Replacing the window does not replace the process holding your running agents. New hosts already contain the earlier bounded-read fix. The synthetic-agent fixture triggered lookup despite having no conversations; its old hosts showed CPU bursts. Source inspection makes the old lookup a plausible cause, but this run did not profile those bursts. Restarting the live host would interrupt its terminals, so it was preserved.

sections.heading: 06 Where I stopped
sections.text:
Keep the measured reuse 
Recommendation: keep the narrow text cache and hidden screen-event filter. The drawing reduction repeated across launch orders and busy workloads. The hidden filter removes screen callbacks and reduces CPU in the plain-program control; the agent workload remains uncertain. 

 Keep the current hidden clock 
Recommendation: retain the one-second check. Lengthening it risks slower attention and completion updates; these changes remove work without that exchange. 

 Use concrete rollback signals 
Stale text on activation, a selection that fails to repaint, or repeatable CPU growth in the same stress test would invalidate this release. The previous version remains available for a GUI-only rollback. 

The release replaces the window while the existing terminal host keeps running. The preceding version remains available for rollback; the local delivery copy records the completed installation.
